title: Kornblut v. Chevron Oil Co. — Court of Appeals
lead: A widow’s roadside-assistance verdict has been dismissed on appeal; the highest court adopts the contract-remedy limitation while a dissenter would revive an undertaking-based theory.

actors.name: The motorist
actors.role: Disabled driver who changed a tire after assistance failed to arrive and later died.

actors.name: The widow
actors.role: Plaintiff recovering at trial under a third-party-beneficiary theory.

actors.name: Chevron Oil Company and its roadside-service contractor
actors.role: Defendants whose contractual service and protective undertaking were at issue.

proceedings: A jury awarded damages to the widow.
The Appellate Division reversed and dismissed in 1978.
In 1979, the Court of Appeals affirmed with costs,6–1; Fuchsberg would reverse and remit for factual review.
limits: This is the 1979 highest-court stage, which adopts Hopkins’s earlier reasons. Fuchsberg’s agency-and-undertaking theory is dissent, and his proposed disposition was remittal for appellate consideration of facts, not automatic restoration of the jury award.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: Contracted help fails to reach a stranded driver
sections.cue: How did the failure to respond lead to the widow’s claim?
paragraphs: A motorist became disabled on a limited-access highway and received no contracted roadside assistance despite repeated reports and assurances. After more than three hours without help in extreme summer heat, he changed his tire himself, suffered a myocardial infarction, and died twenty-eight days later.

His widow sued Chevron Oil Company and its roadside-service contractor. A jury awarded damages on a third-party-beneficiary contract theory. The service arrangement was exclusive and promised a thirty-minute response, features that later became important to the dissent’s assessment of reliance and risk.

sources.pinpoint: Underlying action and dissent; 62 A.D.2d 832–838;48 N.Y.2d 854–856

sections.title: The first appeal recognizes service obligations but limits consequential recovery
sections.cue: Which reasons did the highest court adopt?
paragraphs: In 1978, the Appellate Division reversed the trial judgment and dismissed the action. Justice Hopkins’s opinion regarded the service evidence as sufficient to support breach but held the personal-injury and death losses outside the contemplated contractual responsibility. It recognized particular benefits for motorists, including regulated charges and refunds for overcharges, while rejecting this consequential recovery under contract foreseeability principles.

The widow sought review in the New York Court of Appeals. Its majority affirmed expressly for Hopkins’s reasons, rather than issuing a new extended analysis or adopting Justice Martuscello’s separate appellate concurrence. The adopted rationale did not say that motorists had no beneficiary rights under any provision of the arrangement.

sources.pinpoint: Case reaching the Court of Appeals and adopted reasons;48 N.Y.2d 854;62 A.D.2d 835–839

sections.title: Fuchsberg sees a protective undertaking carrying a possible duty beyond the contract remedy
paragraphs: Justice Fuchsberg dissented. Relying on Restatement (Second) of Agency § 354, he reasoned that an agent undertaking necessary protective action could be liable for physical harm caused by reliance and an unexcused failure to act creating a foreseeable unreasonable risk. Contract terms alone did not exhaust responsibility for undertaking protection and then failing to provide it.

He considered five elements: necessary protective action, reliance, unexcused nonperformance, unreasonable risk and awareness. A stranded vehicle on a fast, limited-access highway needed protection. Exclusivity and the thirty-minute promise supported reliance; a delay exceeding three hours was far from promised performance. Whether the failure was excusable should be for a jury. Breakdowns, restricted access and motorists of limited physical vigor could make self-help dangerous, and the agreement’s concern for public safety supported awareness of that danger.

Fuchsberg also distinguished the earlier Moch case, which concerned hydrant water furnished directly to a city. Here highway users received and paid for the service themselves. He viewed contract, agency and tort principles as interrelated and considered the widow’s showing sufficient for a prima facie case.

sections.title: The six-to-one affirmance leaves dismissal in place
sections.cue: How did the actual remedy differ from the dissent’s proposal?
paragraphs: On November 27, 1979, the Court of Appeals affirmed with costs. Chief Judge Cooke and Judges Jasen, Gabrielli, Jones, Wachtler and Meyer concurred; Fuchsberg alone dissented.

Fuchsberg would have reversed and remitted to the Appellate Division for consideration of the facts. He did not propose immediately entering the jury judgment without that review. His position did not prevail: the action remained dismissed for the adopted reasons, and the Court of Appeals neither awarded fresh damages nor ordered his proposed remittal.
